description: Community can be established and enhanced through communication with one another. Kalinda Fisher is the founder of Advocate Market Research and Executive Director of The Great Reset. After moving to Nashville in 2007, Kalinda kept building Advocate while leaning into her favorite work: creating spaces where people feel heard. When she’s not facilitating a focus group or hosting a dialogue, you’ll find her with her family, a good book, or chasing the next great cup of coffee. A sua experiência pessoal como pai de duas crianças neurodivergentes transformou profundamente a sua visão sobre inteligência, inclusão e o verdadeiro papel da tecnologia na sociedade.

description:
What is the true measure of a life left behind? For generations, society has taught us that legacy is a currency counted in accumulated wealth, inherited land, or a family name passed down strictly through sons. But these traditional metrics often cost us our authenticity, our emotional intelligence, and our progress.

In this insightful and deeply personal TED talk, Dr. Sassi Malik Sher challenges us to look beyond material inheritance. By sharing the powerful story of how her own father defied intense cultural pressures to champion his five daughters, refusing to let outdated traditions dictate their worth, she illustrates how a single person's intent can create a profound ripple effect across generations.

True legacy isn’t a passive inheritance; it is an active choice. It is found in the invisible scripts we write for our children, the emotional freedom we allow our sons, and the spaces we carve out for true equality. This talk is an urgent call to action for the youth to stop acc
title: The Currency of Legacy Beyond Wealth and Names | Dr. Sassi Malik Sher | TEDxSKZMDC Lahore

From silent battles, loneliness, jealousy, fake friendships, and overthinking — to discovering strength, patience, and self-worth, Grade 9 student Madeeha Fatima Zabeeulla brings a deeply emotional and relatable TEDx talk: *“It Is Not Easy to Survive.”*

description:
How far can the ripples of a single defiant act travel? Growing up in a house where literature was a sanctuary from trauma, Talha Siddal found solace in a forgotten Brazilian resistance song on the back of an old book. Years later, he discovered that these words had survived a dictatorship to comfort a frightened child seven oceans away. In this deeply moving talk, he explores the unseen life of the things we leave behind. He reminds us that our words, our resistance, and our smallest acts of empathy cast long, unpredictable echoes that can save a life centuries into the future. From stethoscope to storytelling Dr. Talha’s journey speaks of resilience, identity, and meaning.
Join us as we welcome a voice that bridges medicine, language, and poetry to TEDxSKZMDC. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

In this moving and deeply reflective talk, civil servant Usman Arif challenges us to rethink the concept of legacy. Moving from his early days as an unselected university student at UET to facing the chaotic frontlines of the devastating 2022 floods and intense cyclone evacuations as an Assistant Commissioner, Usman shares the pivotal moments that shaped his life. He argues that a meaningful legacy is built on a simple three-part framework: executing small tasks with relentless consistency, acting with radical honesty in our daily duties, and extending a helping hand to others.

Jessica Neafie is an Assistant Professor of Political Science and International Relations at Nazarbayev University and Director of Undergraduate Studies in the Department of Political Science and International Relations. Her research focuses on Central Asian international relations, multipolarity, energy politics, and China’s engagement in the region, combining computational and qualitative methods to study global political change. In this talk, Nived Lakshman challenges the traditional model of suicide prevention in schools, arguing that adults often overlook the subtle warning signs that students recognize instantly. He proposes both an anonymous, peer‑to‑peer system that empowers teenagers to work alongside administrators to identify and respond to signs of crisis and for further inclusion in student health curriculums. Drawing from a personal moment when his own hesitation to act had painful consequences, he illustrates how dangerous silence can be. Ultimately, he makes the case that teenagers possess an unmatched understanding of their own social dynamics, and by equipping them with safe, structured channels to intervene, schools can activate their most powerful resource for saving young lives.

The hidden ingredient is Belonging Capital: the access, sponsorship, and identity that come from community, and that open doors no credential alone can unlock. Drawing on his journey as an immigrant from Nigeria navigating a new country, Dr. Nnamdi Ihenacho shows how the people who believed in him, vouched for him, and refused to let him quit made the difference between a wall and a breakthrough. His call to action is simple: acknowledge the village that built you -- and turn around to build one for someone else. Dr. Nnamdi Ihenacho stepped into the United States in 2010 carrying two suitcases, a master’s admission letter, and the quiet conviction that hard work would be the master key to every locked door. description: This talk draws a powerful line from the Atlanta Race Massacre of 1906 to today’s technological revolution, revealing a recurring pattern of Black innovation followed by systemic destruction. It highlights how thriving Black economies—from Atlanta to Tulsa Race Massacre and beyond—were dismantled through misinformation, violence, and policy, framing these events as intentional economic sabotage rather than isolated racial conflict. Expanding globally, it connects these injustices to exploitation in places like Haiti and across Africa. The talk then shifts to the present, warning that artificial intelligence and quantum computing risk repeating this cycle if marginalized communities remain excluded from ownership. Despite contributing data, culture, and resources, Black communities are underrepresented in decision-making spaces. title: The Revolution Will Be Coded for African Diaspora | Christine White, Esq. | TEDxCollierHeights

“History is a Feedback Loop,” a talk by Sterling Johnson, explores how culture and history shape the future through the lens of Atlanta and the historic Black community of Collier Heights. Johnson argues that culture preserves collective memory while history provides the context needed to understand where society is headed. Without these guides, innovation often repeats patterns of exploitation rather than creating true progress.
Tracing history from early communal societies to colonization, industrialization, and the rise of artificial intelligence, Johnson shows how each wave of innovation has produced both advancement and inequality. Atlanta embodies this tension: it is a global center of Black culture and resilience while also confronting gentrification and economic disparity.

Through the story of Collier Heights—built by and for Black families—Johnson highlights the power of community vision and self-determination. He ultimately calls for a values-driven approach to innovation,
title: History is a Feedback Loop | Sterling Johnson | TEDxCollierHeights

“Edge of a Universe,” a talk by Floyd Hall, reflects on Atlanta as a city at a critical turning point—caught between its past identity and its rapidly evolving future. Hall explores the tension between “Old Atlanta” and “New Atlanta,” highlighting how legacy communities, longtime residents, and cultural stewards coexist with waves of development, migration, and change.
He emphasizes that the city’s future cannot be left to chance or market forces alone. Instead, it requires a conscious, collective decision by those who know Atlanta and those who are just arriving to shape it intentionally. Hall calls for shared responsibility across generations and communities to preserve cultural memory, protect historic neighborhoods, and ensure that growth does not come at the expense of displacement or erasure.

“Your Life Is Your Closet,” a talk by Mo Ivory, uses the metaphor of a closet to explore personal growth, reinvention, and self-awareness. Ivory compares life to a wardrobe that must be intentionally curated—keeping what fits, removing what no longer serves you, and adding pieces that elevate who you are becoming.
She emphasizes the importance of foundation pieces, likening them to the core skills, values, and experiences that ground us. Just as a well-fitting suit remains a staple, these foundational elements provide confidence and stability as life evolves.
The “remix” represents our ability to reinvent ourselves again and again. Ivory encourages letting go of outdated beliefs, habits, and expectations—what she calls “fast fashion”—in order to make space for growth. Her message is clear: transformation is not something to fear, but something to design.
By building a strong foundation, we gain the freedom to continuously redefine ourselves with intention, courage, and authenticity. C

description: This talk reflects on identity, global exposure, and India’s changing role in the world through the lens of personal experience, education, and cultural transformation. The session examines India’s shift from being viewed primarily as a support economy to becoming a global force in innovation, leadership, culture, and creativity. Blending personal stories with larger societal observations, the talk encourages young people to embrace their identity as a strength, engage with the world confidently, and recognise their role in shaping India’s global perception and future influence.
